opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what surprised me was how little I had to do. I basically just told it, "Hey, I think I have Sonos speakers somewhere on the network, can you figure it out?" And it went off and did a scan of the local network, found the devices, figured out they were Sonos, and then went looking for how you actually talk to them. It discovered there's a local API, poked at the endpoints, and within a few minutes it was playing music in the kitchen. I didn't write a single line of code.

The thing that got me was that I've been through the experience of setting this stuff up the old way. You download the app, you make an account, you fight with the pairing, and every device has its own little walled-garden app. Here the agent just treats all of it as "there's a thing on the network, let me read about it and figure out how to drive it." It felt like the whole layer of apps is kind of unnecessary in this world. The software should really be exposing APIs that agents can use, and the human-facing UI becomes almost an afterthought.

And it was a little bit eerie too, in a fun way. You watch it reasoning through the problem, trying something, getting an error, adjusting, and you realize this is exactly what I would have done if I'd spent an afternoon on it, except it took a few minutes and I was off making coffee. So it's a small example, but it's one of those moments where you feel the shape of the future. Your house becomes something you just talk to, and the agent glues everything together for you.

r001.rationale: The response conveys surprise that a vague request led the agent to find the Sonos devices and play music within minutes, but it does not communicate that this took roughly three prompts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of those moments where I just sat there kind of stunned. I had Dobby running on a little box in my house, and I basically just said, "hey, are there any speakers on the network?" And I did not tell it anything about Sonos. I didn't give it an API key, I didn't give it documentation, nothing. And it just went off and did an mDNS scan, found the devices, figured out they were Sonos, found the local HTTP endpoints, read the responses, and then it's like, "I found four speakers, the living room one is playing something, do you want me to pause it?" And it just worked.

And the thing that surprised me wasn't really that it could do it. I sort of expected that the capability was there in principle. What surprised me was how much of what I thought of as "integration work" just evaporated. Like, historically, if you wanted your software to talk to your speakers, some human had to sit down and write the Sonos plugin. Someone had to read the docs, handle the edge cases, maintain it when the firmware changed. There's this whole long tail of glue code that the entire home automation ecosystem is built on. And the agent just doesn't need any of that. It reads the network the way a curious engineer would. It pokes at things, it reads the error messages, it tries again.

The second thing, honestly, was that it was kind of sloppy in a very human way. It found a speaker in my office that I had forgotten was even plugged in. And it misidentified one of them at first, thought it was a different room, and then corrected itself after it played a test tone and I told it where I heard it. So it's not this perfectly clean system. It's more like having a very eager intern who's on your wifi. Which is also a little bit terrifying when you think about it, because the same curiosity that finds your speakers will find everything else too. I had to think pretty hard about what it's actually allowed to touch.

But the broader point for me is that this is what "software 3.0" looks like at the level of a house. The integration layer is no longer code that somebody wrote in advance. It's something that gets discovered and synthesized on the fly, in context, by the model. And I think a lot of people haven't fully internalized how much of the existing software stack is just that glue, and what happens when it goes away.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes discovering Sonos speakers and playing a test tone, but does not say the agent turned the vague request into actual music playback in roughly three prompts.

astra-6.text:
What surprised me was how little I had to specify. I basically said, “Hey, I think there’s a Sonos system on the network. Can you figure out how to play music?” And Dobby went off and figured out how to discover the speakers and control them. I didn’t have to find a particular integration and wire everything together myself.

That’s the interesting shift for me. You describe the outcome you want, and the agent figures out the plumbing. All these devices already have interfaces, but historically you needed a human to read the documentation and write the glue code. Now that work can happen on demand, as part of fulfilling a request. Your house starts to feel like something you can talk to.

r001.rationale: The response describes a vague request and Dobby discovering and controlling the Sonos speakers, but it does not say music actually played or that this happened in roughly three prompts.

sol-6.1.text:
What surprised me was how little I had to specify. I asked Dobby to play some music, and it figured out that there were Sonos speakers on the network, figured out how to talk to them, and got music playing. I hadn’t explicitly set up a Sonos integration for it.

That’s a very different feeling from traditional home automation, where you’re the one connecting everything and defining all the actions in advance. Here, you give it the outcome you want, and it can work out some of the machinery in between. Your house starts to feel like something you can talk to.

r001.rationale: The response says Dobby inferred that Sonos speakers were on the network and started music from a broad request, but it does not convey that this happened in roughly three prompts.
